parts.title: The Origins of Cinema
parts.subtitle: The 19th-century inventions which led to the birth of the movies
parts.article:
The Origins of Cinema

A Ask most people when the movies began and they will point to the 1890s, but many historians trace the story back to 1824. In that year the British physician Peter Mark Roget described a curious property of human sight: when a series of still pictures is shown to the eye in quick succession, the brain holds each image for a fraction of a second, so that the pictures appear to blend into continuous movement. This effect, later known as 'persistence of vision', was the principle behind every device that followed.

B The most successful of the early devices was the Zoetrope, created in 1834 by another Briton, the mathematician William George Horner. It consisted of a hollow drum, turned by means of a crank. Around the inner surface of the drum ran a strip of paper carrying a sequence of drawings or paintings, each showing a slightly different stage of an action. Cut into the wall of the drum, at regular intervals, were narrow vertical slits. When the drum was spun and the viewer looked through the slits, the pictures inside appeared to move. Sold as a toy from the 1860s onwards, the Zoetrope remained popular for decades.

C Photography, which arrived in 1839, soon replaced hand-drawn images. In 1861 Coleman Sellers, an engineer from Philadelphia, patented the Kinematoscope, a device which presented a sequence of stereoscopic (3D) photographs on glass plates, mounted in order inside a viewing cabinet. Nine years later, in the same city, the inventor Henry Renno Heyl went a step further and put his pictures on a screen. On 5 February 1870, at the Academy of Music in Philadelphia, Heyl used a machine he called the Phasmatrope to show an audience of around 1,500 people a series of photographs of dancers. Projected in rapid succession, the pictures created a convincing illusion of motion.

D Meanwhile, in France, Charles Emile Reynaud had been working on an improved version of the Zoetrope. His Praxinoscope, devised in 1877, did away with the slits altogether; in their place Reynaud fixed a ring of mirrors at the centre of the drum, so that the spinning pictures were reflected to the viewer as a bright and steady image. Two years later the British-born photographer Eadweard Muybridge produced the Zoopraxiscope. This was a true projector: images printed around the edge of a disc were thrown onto a screen as the disc turned, and a whole room could watch the result.

E All of these machines, however, were essentially animations – clever tricks that fooled the eye. True motion pictures, in which real movement is recorded and then replayed, could only come about once a camera existed that could take photographs fast enough. The first real progress was made in the 1880s by Etienne-Jules Marey, a Paris physiologist who wanted to understand how animals and people move. In 1882 he built a camera shaped like a rifle which could take twelve photographs per second, and he later refined the design until it could record as many as thirty images a second. Marey called the results chronophotographs, and it was the speed at which they were recorded that made them so revolutionary.

F Marey's cameras produced a handful of images at a time, but a film would need thousands. In 1888 Louis Le Prince, a Frenchman working in the English city of Leeds, built and patented a camera that used long rolls of paper coated with photographic emulsion; two short fragments of the films he shot with it still survive. The following year the American George Eastman offered a far more practical material – a flexible, transparent roll of celluloid film. Between them, Muybridge, Marey, Le Prince and Eastman had supplied all the ingredients from which cinema could be made.

G It was at Thomas Edison's laboratory in New Jersey that the ingredients were first combined. In November 1890 Edison's British assistant, William Dickson, devised a simple but ingenious motor-powered camera known as the Kinetograph. Its most important feature was a sprocket system of Dickson's own design: the teeth of a rotating wheel engaged with holes punched along both edges of the 35mm-wide film, pulling it through the camera and holding each frame still for an instant in front of the shutter. The Kinetograph was heavy, fixed in one position and needed a great deal of light, and its bulky electric motor was soon abandoned in favour of a lightweight hand-crank mechanism. But although the motor itself did not last, the Kinetograph's film format and its method of advancing the film set the standard for the motion picture cameras that would be used for the next century.

H Dickson also designed an early viewing machine, the Kinetoscope: a tall cabinet in which a loop of film ran continuously past a lamp, watched from above by a single customer. In its earliest form the film was wrapped around a cylinder, and it was on this cylinder version that Dickson shot his first experimental test film, Monkeyshines No. 1 – a few seconds of a laboratory assistant waving his arms about. It is the only film from the cylinder Kinetoscope to have survived, and is generally regarded as the first motion picture ever produced on photographic film in the United States. The Kinetoscope's design, however, meant that only one person could watch at a time.

I Meanwhile in Lyon, France, the brothers Louis and Auguste Lumière, whose family firm manufactured photographic plates, were following Edison and Dickson's work with great interest. Rather than copy the Kinetoscope, they created a multi-purpose device which combined a camera, a printer and a projector in one lightweight box that could be carried by hand. They patented it in February 1895 as the Cinématographe. Commercially it proved far more profitable than the Edison model, because a large number of spectators could watch the same film on a big screen at the same time. On 28 December 1895, in the Salon Indien of the Grand Café in Paris, the Lumières presented the first commercial exhibition of a projected motion picture to a paying public. The programme consisted of ten short films, including one of workers leaving the Lumière factory. The word 'cinema' itself comes from the name of their machine, and that December evening is generally regarded as the moment the movies were born.

analyses.content: 题目问3D图像是展示在什么介质上，原文明确指出这些3D照片是展示在玻璃板（glass plates）上的。

题目问这台机器给观众展示了什么样的错觉，原文对应指出快速投影的图片创造了令人信服的运动（motion）错觉。
你可能会被原文前面的dancers干扰，但dancers是照片里拍的内容，而illusion of后面接的必须是照片动起来后产生的视觉效果。

questions.question: The advantage of Etienne-Jules Marey’s invention was the speed with which it could record images.

analyses.content: 题目说这项发明的优势在于记录图像的速度，原文提到正是它记录图像的速度（speed）让它具有如此革命性的意义，表述完全一致。

questions.question: William Dickson’s system of powering a movie camera with a motor was used for a great many years.

analyses.content: 题目说马达驱动系统被使用了好多年，而原文明确指出笨重的电动机“很快就被废弃了（soon abandoned）”，两者意思完全相反。

In November 1890 Edison's British assistant, William Dickson, devised a simple but ingenious motor-powered camera known as the Kinetograph. Its most important feature was a sprocket system of Dickson's own design: the teeth of a rotating wheel engaged with holes punched along both edges of the 35mm-wide film, pulling it through the camera and holding each frame still for an instant in front of the shutter. The Kinetograph was heavy, fixed in one position and needed a great deal of light, and its bulky electric motor was soon abandoned in favour of a lightweight hand-crank mechanism.

questions.question: Several movies made for the cylinder Kinetoscope are still in existence today.

analyses.content: 题目说有“好几部（Several）”为该机器制作的电影留存至今，但原文明确指出“只有那一部（the only film）”存活了下来。
你可能会因为看到“survived”就觉得对，做判断题时一定要精准核对题目（Several）和原文（only）在数量概念上是否矛盾。

In its earliest form the film was wrapped around a cylinder, and it was on this cylinder version that Dickson shot his first experimental test film, Monkeyshines No. 1 – a few seconds of a laboratory assistant waving his arms about. It is the only film from the cylinder Kinetoscope to have survived, and is generally regarded as the first motion picture ever produced on photographic film in the United States.

questions.question: The Lumiere brothers’ invention was used to make and show movies.

analyses.content: 题目说卢米埃尔兄弟的发明被用来制作和放映电影，原文明确写了他们的设备结合了摄像机（能够制作）和投影仪（能够放映）的功能。

Rather than copy the Kinetoscope, they created a multi-purpose device which combined a camera, a printer and a projector in one lightweight box that could be carried by hand. They patented it in February 1895 as the Cinématographe.

questions.question: None of the audience at the Salon Indien in December 1895 had ever seen a motion picture before.

analyses.content: 题目说1895年12月在场的观众以前绝对没看过电影，原文只提到这是“面向公众的首次商业放映”，完全没提这批观众私底下或者之前有没有看过类似的东西。
你可能看到原文说那天晚上是“电影诞生的时刻”就脑补大家肯定都没看过，但这只是历史视角的宏观评价，并不能无中生有地推断出在场每个观众的过往经历。
